results.title: Another player involved in college eligibility suit gets cut by an NFL team - San Francisco Chronicle
results.content: Defensive lineman Jack Pyburn was waived by the Tampa Bay Buccaneers on Sunday and could be the latest player who tries to go back to college after spending time in an NFL camp. He'll become a free agent if he's not picked up and is among the players granted a temporary restraining order by a Louisiana court earlier this month that would make them eligible to return to college athletics. Four other players who spent time on NFL rosters this offseason before being cut were also part of the case: former LSU running back TJ Harden, former Mississippi tight end Dae'Quan Wright, former Ole Miss defensive lineman Zxavian Harris and former Oregon State running back Anthony Hankerson. Here's a look at some of the players who spent time in NFL camps this summer and now might return to college:. Pyburn originally signed as an undrafted free agent with Tampa Bay in May. He played in two exhibition games and led the NFL with four sacks in the preseason.

results.title: Metropolitan Museum of Art cancels planned Met Gala exhibit on fashion designer John Galliano - San Francisco Chronicle
results.content: # Metropolitan Museum of Art cancels planned Met Gala exhibit on fashion designer John Galliano. NEW YORK (AP) — The Metropolitan Museum of Art is canceling its planned exhibit honoring British designer John Galliano, which had led to severe backlash in the Jewish community and beyond because of the designer’s past antisemitic and racist statements. “Following thoughtful discussions with John Galliano, we have together decided not to proceed with the exhibition," Max Hollein, director and CEO of the museum, announced in a statement. The designer joined in the statement, saying: “After much reflection and discussion with The Met and all those involved, I have decided, with great sadness, that it is best for the exhibition not to take place at this time. He was to become only the third living designer to be the subject of a solo show at the Met's Costume Institute.

results.title: What counts as art? This S.F. exhibition offers more than 70 answers - San Francisco Chronicle
results.content: His historic exhibition at the Smithsonian that year — “Objects: USA,” featuring more than 500 works by ceramicists, weavers, quilters, woodworkers and artists specializing in metal, glass, enamel, mosaic and more — helped shift that line of thinking. Almost six decades years later, the Museum of Craft and Design is revisiting the concept, with a new “Objects: USA” with more than 70 pieces that break down the silos of art, craft and design. Now he takes center stage in S.F. Some works, such as Wendell Castle’s “Tongue,” a shiny end table with an angled base resembling a children’s slide, come from the original “Objects: USA.” Others, like a lamp made by Jolie Ngo, as fuzzy and colorful and wacky as a Dr. Seuss illustration, hail from our era. A Michigan native whose childhood also took her to Tennessee and Texas, she holds a BA in theater studies from Yale and an MA in drama from San Francisco State.

results.title: How Yayoi Kusama’s San Francisco triumph became an SFMOMA reckoning - San Francisco Chronicle
results.content: For many Bay Area museumgoers, Yayoi Kusama’s first solo Northern California exhibition at the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art in 2023 became the backdrop for selfies and Instagram reels. Now, with news of Kusama’s death in Tokyo at 97 on Aug. 14, confirmed by the Yayoi Kusama Studio this week, the controversy that shadowed that SFMOMA show is inseparable from her local legacy. But the show also ignited questions over racist language in Kusama’s writings spanning several decades, placing the Japanese artist at the center of a predicament many arts institutions across the country were grappling with over how to present the work of acclaimed artists with problematic pasts. But for all her success, she could not tamp down the simmering controversy that came to a boil in San Francisco on the cusp of “Yayoi Kusama: Infinite Love” at SFMOMA in October 2023. Tony Bravo is the Chronicle’s arts and culture columnist.

results.title: A 95-foot artwork is about to transform this historic San Francisco building - San Francisco Chronicle
results.content: A 95-foot animated artwork is about to transform a historic Market Street building into one of downtown San Francisco’s largest canvases, launching a new public art partnership among three museums. The Yerba Buena Illuminated initiative will debut on Tuesday, Aug. 25, with Los Angeles artist Jennifer Steinkamp’s “It’s a nice day for a white wedding” at 785 Market St. The digital art work’s title is inspired by Billy Idol’s 1982 hit song “White Wedding” and will project a cascade of animated red, white and yellow wedding flowers on the Beaux-Arts–style Humboldt Bank Building. It comes from the collection of the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, one of the three cultural institutions collaborating with Yerba Buena Partnership, a neighborhood community benefit district. “This installation will be a powerful symbol of the vibrancy and creativity that defines San Francisco and yet another reason for San Franciscans and visitors to enjoy the public spaces, cultural institutions, and all the Yerba Buena area has to offer.”.
